en: Has your father Shaatemir died?
Have the people wailed and the nation cried out?
Has someone buried your father?!
When your slave comes pleading, calling you kin
And bearing no grudge,
You rage and threaten;
When your servant comes, you change your face
And rave as though your mother’s kin
Had all been massacred.
Before, you spoiled my temper;
You roused in me a rage no cudgel could quell.
Without cause you spoiled my temper,
Tormented every spoonful of my blood,
And made my whole soul boil!
Why did you come shouting and raging
To speak such cutting words?
Has some great slaughter befallen you?
Why did you provoke my wrath?
You are only a woman, yet you worked yourself up;
Had I left you to your own devices,
You raged as though you would devour me.
You shouted in anger,
And before even your husband, woman,
You summoned your executioners.
You fouled your tongue and made it a sheath,
Raised a clamor and started strife,
Calling me a fugitive son of the khagan,
A flesh-born slave of the bloodthirsty one;
You drive my blood from its course,
Shrieking your ceaseless abuse,
And thus bring about my end.
Of the fugitive who came from the khagan’s realm—
He thrust his hand inside her,
And the black blood of her heart
He scooped up in both hands and swallowed:
“Now my vengeance is sated;
Now what died in me has revived,
And my extinguished fire is kindled!”
While Külchoro was doing this,
Before Kanchoro could prepare against him,
Before Kanchoro could summon his courage,
Before he could unleash his fierce wrath,
Before his executioners could rush like wind
And reach him and surround him,
Before the people cried out and the nation panicked,
Before they could offer him as a sacrifice,
Before anyone could utter a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Aichürök, daughter of Akun,
Ready to die if death had come,
To stand as protector of Külchoro,
Her mighty mountain of support—
The wretched fairy-like beauty
Was torn by many thoughts;
Tears poured from her eyes,
Her heart boiled like embers.
Having donned black for the conflict,
How could she stand still?
Her wrist-thick hair came loose,
And tears flowing from both eyes
Streamed below her two breasts.
If conflict suddenly erupted,
If fate decreed his death,
How could she endure the loss
Of the brother-in-law who protected her?
His malice was deep, his venom strong,
A bloodstained destroyer of peoples,
That resourceful kinsman Kanchoro,
Yet his stature was that of a hero.
If the poor eagle were attacked,
If my brother-in-law were suddenly caught
In bitter, calamitous strife—
While she thought thus, Külchoro
Was seized by towering rage.
At the shrew upon the throne
He charged and swiftly reached her.
The warrior-lion, matchless in speed,
Seized that exceedingly venomous infidel
With a hero’s might,
Grabbing her by her black hair.
By the hearth stood a stone trivet;
Onto that stone trivet
He lifted and flung the woman.
The warrior upheld by the spirit Shay
Revealed himself a true lion;
When he struck the woman unerringly,
She split in two through the middle.
Its haft was steel, its point was sharp,
Black hardening ran along its edge,
Its blade gaped a handspan wide
And spread blood wherever it struck.
Laid upon grass, it set it aflame;
Those it struck died at once.
Its crown was like a mace’s fist,
And its haft was fashioned of steel;
When swung, its edge glowed red,
And no place it touched remained unharmed.
So that its victim would fester and rot,
So that death would overtake
All whom it touched without exception,
Bölökbay the master smith
Tempered it sixty times
In a dragon’s venom
And honed its edge keen.
Saying its blade was hard as crystal,
He polished it again and again;
The noble smith Bölökbay
Forged it together with Davut.
He snatched up and swung Aibalta,
The battle-axe left by great-hearted Manas,
And from the shrieking woman
He struck off the head.
Her heart aching, her insides boiling,
Distraught and burning with grief,
Tensed like a steed beneath a hero,
Her eyes dimmed and reddened,
Her whip-slim waist twisting,
To confront Kanchoro,
To stand as protector
For her brother-in-law, the gray-maned warrior,
And, if she found the chance,
To subdue the mad Kanchoro,
To destroy him and spill his blood,
To do all that she knew how,
To drink his blood by the spoonful,
The heroically formed Aichürök
Struck out in front.
Following behind them
Came the finest of the long-haired,
The worthiest of women,
The purest in a flowing gown,
The foremost wife ever born,
Your aged mother Kanykey,
Coming into this horde
To take her ancient vengeance
On blood-spilling Kanchoro,
To prove her breast milk pure
By offering him as a sacrifice,
To make his noble head bow,
To drink Kanchoro’s blood,
And swiftly cut off his head.
That old conflict held many torments,
And she came to take vengeance in full.
The reason for her vengeance was
That he had heaped endless humiliation on her,
Beating and stretching her out like a hide.
He had tied her by the waist
To a barren cow’s calf and had her dragged,
Thus inflicting his punishment.
Her aged flesh was torn apart,
Not a spoonful of blood remained,
And your mother had no strength left.
She came to hew his executioners into seven pieces
And spill their furious blood.
Dragon-like Kanchoro—
Of all the property and boundless wealth remaining,
She came to demand what was hers.
Moon-faced Aichürök,
A wonder unlike any mortal,
Of serene and stately bearing,
Precious as a fairy,
Whose curse never missed its mark,
Whose wrath was never spent in vain—
The formidable woman Aichürök
Gathered her dear hair, long as river grass,
And bound it tightly atop her head.
The impetuous, ill-fated woman
Put on a man’s attire.
“I shall stand guard for the warrior,” she said,
Her supreme courage showing,
Springing forward like a doe,
Stretching tall as Surayyl,
Striding jauntily and eagerly,
Arching like a white doe,
Rushing on without sparing her life,
Driven by a furious spirit.
Her life, merely held in trust,
She staked upon a single hair.
She broke away in fury,
Her heroic courage plain,
Her eyes dimmed, her heart aflame;
Though many cried out, she strode on.
When courage rose, the head was forfeit,
And from her currant-dark eyes
Tears mingled with blood streamed down.
She began the true battle;
Straining every sinew, the poor woman
Cast away her fly-like life.
She summoned fierce resolve;
This raging woman cast her precious life
Without hesitation upon the black earth.
His blood draining, he ground his teeth.
Her heart boiled like fire:
“Can an aged soul live forever?
Has not the mischief
Of wretched Chachykey gone far enough?
Despairing of her fly-like life,
Behind Aichürök
Kanykey came running.
“Kanchoro has always been fierce.
My dear son Külchoro
Has always been tenderhearted.
If they stand face-to-face,
Thrusting spears and striking with axes,
Battering each other in combat,
Taking up Zulfiqar-like spears,
Driving them into living hearts,
And fighting without measure;
If they begin a dreadful conflict
And stake lives frail as flies
Upon a single hair;
If they begin a slaughtering battle,
When blades are drawn aslant,
The sword will blaze with heat
As they grapple till they are cherry-red—
Such is the ruin of furious war.
If by chance the fatal hour arrives
In a struggle such as this,
Kanchoro, who guarded the horde and ruled the people,
Who mounted and held the golden throne,
Who never suffered torment or humiliation
But grazed freely on broad pastures,
Whose five fingers never lacked grease,
Whose marrow no arrow could pierce—
Black-hearted Kanchoro
Will wage the clash savagely.
By what means will he seize
My only son, my sole protector?
Only lately recovered from slavery,
Grown strong after years of misery,
His shoulders only newly filled out,
My lion was pure steel.
Her darkening eyes became clouded;
The two servants who kept her alive
Stiffened like stakes, palsied,
Their chests rasping,
Their entire bodies
Shuddering beyond control.
Her twelve bones and limbs
Wasted helplessly, wheezing;
Her ten vertebrae and eighty joints
Crackled, swollen with yellow fluid.
Her waist sank and her back bent,
Her stricken body withered.
The old lady remained there
With her body weakened and diminished,
Brought level with the black earth,
Left stooped and bent.
Gripping the doorpost, she ran,
Burning and grieving
At Kanchoro’s wrath.
While divinely protected Külchoro,
Her precious son, still lived,
Kanchoro had humiliated her.
She came to slash him to pieces,
To torture him and bring calamity,
